title: Sue Bryce — Shooting Curves (posing masterclass)
summary: Sue Bryce teaches her system for posing curvy bodies, which she stresses is the same system she uses on every body type. It reduces to three moves applied in order: turn 45 degrees to camera, put the weight on the back foot so the near hip travels away from the lens, and push the chin forward and down - further forward the curvier the subject. Around that she builds arm and hand rules (arms off the torso, elbows pulled back, visible triangles), a 'faux waist' created by placing the hands higher and further in than the true waist, seated and reclining variants on an apple box, and a firm ruling that the camera belongs on the subject's eye line rather than above it. The closing section is not technique: she recounts once shooting two sisters head-and-shoulders only, and identifies the cause as her own body-shame rather than their bodies. Full prose breakdown lives at Visions-ai/knowledge_base/posing_curves.md - this record is the pointer, not a duplicate.

steps.action: Move 1 - turn 45 degrees to camera. Not side-on. Opens the shoulder and pushes it out and back.
Move 2 - weight onto the back foot, pushing the near hip away from the lens; then push the weight into the FRONT of the hip and it travels back further still.
Move 3 - chin forward and down. The signature. The curvier the body, the further forward and down it must go. Client line that sells it: 'feels weird, looks fantastic.'

Camera on the subject's EYE LINE or a touch above - never from up high. Slimming comes from tilting the BODY, not raising the camera; shooting down just makes them look like they are looking up at you.

Shoot the 35mm: slightly wide so focus holds on the face while the body drops away. The 50 reads flatter. EXCEPTION - on a very lean body do not pull the hips away from camera, it makes the head look huge.
Get the arms OFF the torso - arms resting against the body read as one mass with it. Thumbs into the jean pockets relaxes the hands, shapes the elbows and lifts the arms clear.

'Barbie'/tabletop hands: hands out flat as if on a table, then pull the ELBOWS back behind the body. Narrows the whole line and brings the chest forward. Failure mode is pulling the SHOULDERS back too far - pull elbows, not shoulders.
Make triangles. Visible space between arm and body is what reads as slim. Drop a dominant forearm or move inside its line; keep hands low, never stiff or splayed.

The faux waist: people place their hands on their TRUE waist - place them higher and further in instead and invent a waistline, because the eye reads the hands as the waist. Kick the booty back. Watch for pinched fabric.

Kill the double chin: chin forward and down creating visible space between chin and chest line, and push the SHOULDER down - the lower it goes, the longer the neck reads. In a relaxed neck the chin often photographs as raised even when it does not look raised in the room.
Stop rapid blinking by asking the subject to 'slow down your blinks' - naming it creates the awareness that stops it.

Seated: slide the near arm against the thigh and all the way back to define the hourglass; knees together, then knees AND feet away from camera. The further the lower half travels, the longer and slimmer she reads. Do not let the frame fold up.
Apple box against a wall: on the floor she cannot recline because everything shortens the torso. The box lifts her so the body opens and she can take the shoulder back to the wall.

Over-the-shoulder with curves requires a whole-body tip forward - and crucially it is NOT tipping toward the camera, it is tipping forward along her own axis so the shoulder drops and the face angle opens.
Cover-girl frames shot straight into backlight with a reflector bouncing back to the face; black v-flat behind a pale-skinned subject.

The ethic: she once photographed two sisters head-and-shoulders only. They asked why afterwards. The cause was not skill or retouching but her own body-shame at the time - she was judging their bodies through her own. Her ruling: never assume someone is not proud of their body just because you were not proud of yours.

key_takeaways: Three moves, in order, on every body type: 45 degrees to camera, weight on the back foot, chin forward and down - and the curvier the subject the further forward and down the chin goes.
Slimming comes from tilting the body, not from raising the camera. Shoot on the eye line or a touch above; shooting down is the mistake almost everyone makes.
The 35mm is the slimming lens because the body drops away behind the face; the 50 reads flatter. But do not pull a lean subject's hips back - it enlarges the head.
Arms touching the torso read as one mass with it. Elbows pulled back, hands given a job, and visible triangles of space are what actually narrow the body.
The faux waist is the strongest single trick: the eye reads the hands as the waistline, so place them higher and further in than the true waist.
A double chin is eliminated by chin-forward-and-down plus pushing the shoulder down to lengthen the neck - not by raising the camera.
Direct constantly and reset every frame; the client cannot see through the camera and is waiting for guidance. Sculpt rather than shooting hundreds of frames hoping.
The technique exists to serve the person: the goal is not an ideal to conform to, but making each subject look the best they can. People buy photographs in which they themselves look good.
